VERDICT: EXTEND C0004 | `scan_health()` also misreports tool availability on timeout, not just missing binary. Evidence: each runner returns `[]` when `_run_tool()` returns `CompletedProcess(..., returncode=-1, stderr="TIMEOUT")`; `scan_health()` then sets `tools_available[tool_name] = True` because the runner returned normally. This creates the same false “healthy toolchain” signal under a different failure mode. Downstream, insect-brain consumers cannot distinguish “no diagnostics because clean” from “no diagnostics because tool hung”. The existing fix should treat timeout as unavailable/failed execution too, not only NOT_FOUND.

FINDING_ID: F001
SEVERITY: 0.91
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.63
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `evaluate_fix()`’s optional test execution is not sandboxed to the patched codebase; it only changes `cwd` to the temp directory while leaving the original repository and original test targets in place. Evidence: the sandbox contains only `os.path.basename(target_path)` written to `tmpdir`; no package tree or tests are copied. Yet `test_cmd` is executed verbatim via `_run_tool(test_cmd, cwd=tmpdir)`. In the actual integration path from `immune_agents.py`, the command is `["python3", "-m", "pytest", "bench/tests/", ...]`, which resolves against the real repo, not the tempdir-only patched file. For imports such as `bench.endocrine`, Python will load the original source from the repository/package path, so `tests_passed` can report success or failure for unpatched code while the verdict is attributed to the proposed fix.
FOLLOW: This breaks the endocrine layer’s key claimed capability: “sandbox-test proposed fixes”. A fix can be marked SAFE/NEUTRAL even if the patched file would fail tests, because the tests never exercised the patched module. Conversely, a good patch can be marked HARMFUL because unrelated baseline failures in the real repo are observed instead. The interface crosses directly into `immune_agents.run_immune_pipeline()`, which sets `finding.verified = True` for SAFE/NEUTRAL results; that in turn activates the NK bug-closed gate and suppresses future findings as duplicates of a supposedly verified fix. So this is a silently wrong-results path, not just weak validation.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — in `evaluate_fix()`, copy the repo subtree needed for execution into the tempdir and apply the patch at the same relative path, then run `test_cmd` against that temp copy. The simplest sufficient implementation is: determine the project root from `target_path`/`source_paths`, `shutil.copytree()` the relevant `bench/` tree (and tests if separate) into `tmpdir`, patch the copied file in place, and execute tests with `cwd=tmpdir` using paths inside the copy.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F002
SEVERITY: 0.88
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.58
DESCRIPTION: FIND — fix evaluation compares pre-fix diagnostics from the original file against post-fix diagnostics from an isolated temp file with a different import/context environment, so pyright results are not comparable and can be spuriously improved. Evidence: `evaluate_fix()` computes `pre_type_errors = _count_tool_issues(run_pyright, target_path)` on the real file path, then writes only the single patched file to `tmpdir` and computes `new_type_errors = _count_tool_issues(run_pyright, patched_path)`. Pyright analyzes imports/types relative to file location and project context. Moving one file out of its package tree changes import resolution; missing sibling modules/config no longer participate. The comparison therefore conflates “effect of patch” with “effect of removing project context”.
FOLLOW: A patch can appear SAFE because type errors disappear in isolation, or HARMFUL because the moved file loses project configuration and import context. This directly affects `_compute_fix_verdict()` and therefore `immune_agents` stage 4 verified-fix marking. Since verified fixes close bugs in later rounds, a non-comparable baseline/post comparison can lock in false bug closure or reject valid fixes. This undermines end-to-end review correctness.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — run both pre- and post-fix tool checks in the same sandboxed project context. Copy the relevant source tree to `tmpdir`, run all “pre” counts on the copied unmodified file there, patch that copied file, then run the “post” counts on the same copied tree.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F003
SEVERITY: 0.84
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.54
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `_find_target_file()` can select the wrong source file by substring match, causing fix evaluation to patch/evaluate a different file than the finding refers to. Evidence: after extracting `*.py` tokens from description/fix text, it returns the first `sp_path` where `sp_path.endswith(match) or match in sp_path`. The `match in sp_path` branch is overly broad: a token like `endocrine.py` matches any path containing that substring; shorter or partial path mentions can also collide across similarly named files/directories. The function returns on first match, with no ambiguity check.
FOLLOW: If the wrong file is chosen, `_apply_fix_to_source()` may still succeed mechanically and the tool counts/verdict will be attached to the original finding ID. Downstream this creates a false SAFE/HARMFUL result for the wrong artifact, and `immune_agents` may mark the finding verified based on analysis of an unrelated file. That is silent state corruption across the endocrine→immune interface.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — restrict matching to exact basename or exact normalized suffix matches only, and if multiple source paths match, return `None`/UNEVALUABLE instead of picking the first ambiguous path.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F004
SEVERITY: 0.79
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.48
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `_compute_fix_verdict()` can classify a fix as SAFE even when it introduces new issues in one tool, as long as enough issues disappear in other tools to make the summed net negative. Evidence: it computes `total_net = net_type_errors + net_ruff_errors + net_bandit_issues`; if `total_net > 0` => HARMFUL, `total_net < 0` => SAFE. Example: `+1` new Bandit issue, `-2` Ruff issues, `0` type issues yields `total_net = -1` and verdict SAFE, despite a newly introduced security issue. The same masking occurs for any per-tool regression offset by reductions elsewhere.
FOLLOW: This violates the documented SAFE semantics (“no new issues introduced”) and silently approves regressive fixes. In integration, `immune_agents` marks SAFE/NEUTRAL fixes as verified, so a patch that adds a new security or type error can still close a bug if enough unrelated lint issues drop. That directly misleads reviewers and contaminates later dedup/closure logic.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — compute harmfulness per dimension: if any of `net_type_errors`, `net_ruff_errors`, or `net_bandit_issues` is positive, return HARMFUL. Only return SAFE when at least one metric improved and none regressed; otherwise keep existing NEUTRAL/tests logic.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F005
SEVERITY: 0.72
FLAW_CLASS: 4
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.67
DESCRIPTION: FIND — the module advertises fix evaluation as sandboxed and “never modifies actual source”, but the implementation only sandboxes writes, not execution context, and does not evaluate package-level or multi-file fixes at all. Evidence: `_apply_fix_to_source()` operates on one source text string; `evaluate_fix()` writes one basename-only file to tempdir and evaluates that single file. No support exists for preserving relative module paths, applying changes across multiple files, or exercising the copied package graph. This makes the “sandbox-test proposed fixes” capability materially narrower than the interface claims.
FOLLOW: The feature fires for simple single-file text substitutions but is effectively dead/misleading for the common class of fixes that depend on package context, sibling imports, or tests. Downstream systems may trust verdicts as if they represented realistic sandbox execution. In PoC terms this is high because it deceives the human reviewer about what the feature has actually validated.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — narrow the contract in code and logs immediately: mark evaluation UNEVALUABLE unless the target file can be evaluated in a copied project subtree preserving its relative path. This is the simplest fix that prevents false assurance without adding broad refactoring.
VERIFIED: TRUE
